title: Using the open book: chapters, tables and RACI fast
blurb: Find the right chapter, role table or RACI row in under a minute, and know when the book will not help.
question: A question asks who should be accountable for appointing the project management team in starting up a project. You half remember. Where exactly do you look, and how long should it take?

teach.h: The manual is a tool, not a textbook
teach.body: The Practitioner exam is open book: you may use the official PRINCE2 7 Managing Successful Projects book, and you may write notes inside it, but no other material is allowed. The book only saves marks if you can find things fast. Learn its layout so that a RACI row, a product's contents or a role's area of focus is one flick away, and save your reading time for the scenario.
teach.cite: PeopleCert PRINCE2 7 Practitioner syllabus, Exam Overview

head: Chapter
What lives there

teach.caption: Practices run business case (5), organizing (6), plans (7), quality (8), risk (9), issues (10), progress (11). Processes run SU (13), DP (14), IP (15), CS (16), MP (17), SB (18), CP (19).
In each process chapter, table x.1 lists inputs, activities and outputs, table x.2 is the RACI and table x.3 shows the practices applied. Starting up's RACI is table 13.2.

children.edge: Which role is A, R, C or I?
children.label: Process chapter, RACI table

teach.h: Look up to confirm, not to learn
teach.body: The book is fastest for facts that are easy to forget and easy to find: RACI rows, management product headings, activity names and their recommended actions. It is slow for judgement questions, where the answer depends on reading the situation against a principle you should already understand. Decide the verdict first; open the book only to settle the one fact that separates your last two options.

Carrowford City Council's cabinet (scenario S5) gives Andrew Mallory, director of culture, leisure and tourism, the mandate. Andrew asks project manager Kezia Oduya to choose the senior user and senior supplier. A question asks whether this is appropriate. You flick to table 13.2: for 'appoint the project management team', the business layer is accountable, the executive is responsible and the project manager is not involved. So the answer is no: Andrew, as executive, should make the appointments.

teach.h: Preparing your book within the rules
items: Write chapter numbers on the page edges so you can open a process chapter in one move.
Mark every process RACI table (13.2, 14.2 and so on) and every practice roles table.
Add cross-references in the margins, for example beside 2.5 'tolerances: see 11.2.1'.
Keep notes inside the book: loose sheets and other material are not allowed.
Confirm with PeopleCert or your training provider whether your sitting accepts a printed copy, an eBook or index tabs.

teach.text: Classic appointment trap: the business layer appoints the executive and is accountable for both starting up appointments, the executive is responsible for appointing the rest of the project management team, and the project manager is not involved. A project manager choosing the board is a 'No' answer.

items: Only the official manual is allowed; notes inside it are fine, loose material is not.
Process chapters: table x.2 is the RACI, table x.3 the practices applied.
Practice chapters: x.5 products, x.6 roles' areas of focus, x.7 links to principles.
Look up facts (RACI, headings, activities); answer judgement from understanding.
SU appointments: business layer accountable, executive responsible, PM not involved.

summary: You can now find any RACI row, product heading or role's area of focus in the manual quickly, and you know which questions the book helps with. You can also apply the starting up RACI and the business case role responsibilities to the S5 scenario.

A.q: Carrowford City Council's cabinet has issued a mandate for the Carrowford Half Marathon and named Andrew Mallory, the director who holds the events budget, as executive. The project is in starting up a project and the rest of the project management team now needs to be appointed. Which role should be accountable for these appointments?
A.why: For 'appoint the project management team' the business layer is accountable and the executive responsible (13.4.4, table 13.2).

whyNot.0: The executive is responsible for making the appointments, but accountability sits with the business layer.
whyNot.2: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
whyNot.3: The senior user is one of the roles being appointed, not the role accountable for appointing.

A.q: During the Carrowford Half Marathon's build-up stage, the council's leadership asks someone on the project board to show that the forecast £2.5 million of local spending and the 30% share of local entrants are still on track. Which role should do this?
A.why: The senior user specifies the benefits and demonstrates to the business that the forecast benefits are on track to be realized (6.2.4.2).

whyNot.0: The executive owns the business case and secures funding; demonstrating that forecast benefits are on track is the senior user's focus.
whyNot.1: Project assurance monitors the business case for the board; it does not demonstrate benefits to the business.
whyNot.3: The project manager maintains the business case for the executive but is not the board member who demonstrates benefits.

A.q: A candidate meets a question about the Carrowford project: the project manager produces a highlight report and the question asks which roles should be consulted. The candidate is unsure between two options. Where in the manual is the quickest reliable place to check?
options: The roles table in the progress practice chapter
The RACI table in the controlling a stage chapter
The 'manage by exception' principle in chapter 2
The process model overview in chapter 12
A.why: 'Report highlights' is a controlling a stage activity, so its RACI sits in the controlling a stage chapter (table 16.2).

whyNot.0: The progress roles table gives each role's areas of focus, not the RACI for a process activity.
whyNot.2: Chapter 2 explains the principle; it does not list who is consulted in an activity.
whyNot.3: Chapter 12 gives the overall process model, not activity-level RACI.

B.q: On the Carrowford Half Marathon, the cabinet has appointed Andrew Mallory as executive and Kezia Oduya as project manager. Senior user and senior supplier roles still need filling before initiation. Which role should be responsible for appointing them?
B.why: The executive is responsible for appointing the rest of the project management team; the business layer is accountable (13.4.4).

whyNot.0: The business layer is accountable for the appointments; the executive is the role responsible for making them.
whyNot.1: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
whyNot.3: Project assurance is among the roles being appointed; the executive is responsible for appointing it.

B.q: Carrowford's project is in initiating a project. Kezia Oduya is preparing the full business case using the project plan's costs and the event's aggregated risks. Which combination of roles matches the recommended RACI for this activity?
options: Senior user accountable; project manager responsible
B.why: For 'prepare the full business case' the executive is accountable, the project manager responsible and project assurance consulted; the business layer is not involved (15.4.5).

whyNot.1: The business layer is not involved in preparing the full business case.
whyNot.2: The project manager is responsible, not accountable, and support does not prepare it.
whyNot.3: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable for the business case.

B.q: During starting up the Carrowford Half Marathon, Kezia Oduya opens a daily log and gathers lessons from other councils' races before the formal registers exist. A question asks which practice the starting up process is applying when it sets up the daily log. Which practice is it?
B.why: The starting up practices table (13.3) links setting up the daily log and gathering lessons to the progress practice.

whyNot.0: Initial risks are noted in the daily log, but setting up the log itself applies progress.
whyNot.1: The issue register and issue management approach are set up in initiation.
whyNot.2: In starting up, quality covers understanding the quality expectations and requirements.

C.q: In starting up the Carrowford Half Marathon, executive Andrew Mallory asks project manager Kezia Oduya to choose and appoint the senior user and senior supplier, as she knows the race partners best. Is this an appropriate application of the 'appoint the project management team' activity, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM manages the project day to day for the executive
Yes, because the team must reflect business, user and supplier interests
No, because the executive is responsible for appointing the team
No, because the senior supplier is appointed by the supplier itself
C.why: The executive is responsible and the business layer accountable for appointing the project management team; the project manager is not involved (13.4.4).

whyNot.0: True that the PM runs the project day to day, but this does not make appointing the board her task.
whyNot.1: True that all three interests must be represented, but this does not explain who should appoint them.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier is appointed through the executive, not by the supplying organization.

C.q: At the end of Carrowford's planning and approvals stage, Kezia Oduya updates the business case with actual costs, entry numbers so far and the latest sponsorship forecast. Andrew Mallory, the executive, reviews it before the board considers the next stage. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM maintains the case with actuals at each stage end
Yes, because the project manager is accountable for the business case
No, because the senior user maintains the business case during delivery
No, because the business case is frozen once the project is authorized
C.why: Maintaining the business case means the PM updates it at each stage end with progress data and latest forecasts, on behalf of the executive (5.3.1).

whyNot.1: The executive is accountable for the business case; the PM prepares and maintains it.
whyNot.2: The senior user specifies benefits; maintaining the business case is the PM's task for the executive.
whyNot.3: The business case is maintained and checked throughout delivery, not frozen.

C.q: A candidate preparing for the Practitioner exam plans to bring the official manual, with handwritten notes in its margins, and a one-page summary sheet folded inside the cover. Is this an appropriate way to use the open book, and why?
options: Yes, because the exam is open book and notes are permitted
Yes, because the summary sheet is copied from the manual's tables
No, because handwritten notes inside the manual are not permitted
No, because loose material other than the manual is not permitted
C.why: You may write notes inside the official book, but no other material is allowed, so the loose summary sheet must go.

whyNot.0: Notes are permitted inside the book, which does not cover a separate sheet.
whyNot.1: Copying from the manual does not change the rule: loose material is not allowed.
whyNot.2: Notes written inside the book are allowed by the syllabus.

reteach.title: Use the book like a dictionary, not a novel
reteach.question: You would never read a dictionary from page one to find a word. How do you treat the PRINCE2 manual the same way?

blocks.h: Know the shelf, then the page
blocks.body: First decide the shelf: is the question about a principle (chapter 2), a practice (chapters 5 to 11) or a process (chapters 13 to 19)? Then the page: in a process chapter, the RACI is in the responsibilities section near the end; in a practice chapter, the products and the roles table are near the end too. Two moves, not twenty.

steps.label: Read one row
steps.sub: A, R, C, I for your activity

blocks.text: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team. If an option has the PM choosing board members, it is wrong.

explain.body: Chapter 2 holds the principles. Chapters 5 to 11 are the practices in order: business case, organizing, plans, quality, risk, issues, progress. Chapters 13 to 19 are the processes in order: SU, DP, IP, CS, MP, SB, CP.

test.q: On the Carrowford Half Marathon, the corporate risk manager asks how proximity and risk responses should be recorded. A candidate wants the risk practice's management products. Which chapter should she open?
test.why: The risk practice is chapter 9: business case 5, organizing 6, plans 7, quality 8, risk 9.

whyNot.1: Chapter 2 covers the principles, not the risk practice.
whyNot.3: Chapter 12 is the overview of the process model.

test.q: A Carrowford question asks which role should be informed when the board authorizes the next stage. The candidate knows this is a directing a project activity. Which part of chapter 14 gives the answer fastest?
options: The purpose section at the start of the chapter
The list of objectives for directing a project
The RACI table in the responsibilities section
The table of practices applied by the process
test.why: Each process chapter's responsibilities section holds the RACI table (14.2 for directing a project), listing who is informed for each activity.

whyNot.0: The purpose explains why the process exists, not who is informed.
whyNot.1: The objectives describe what the process achieves, not role involvement.
whyNot.3: The practices table links actions to practices, not to RACI roles.

test.q: Carrowford City Council's cabinet issues the mandate for the half marathon. In starting up, someone must be accountable for appointing the executive and the project manager. Which role is it?
test.why: The business layer is accountable for appointing the executive and the project manager; the executive is responsible (13.4.1).

whyNot.0: The executive is responsible in this activity, not accountable.
whyNot.1: The senior user has no part in appointing the executive.
whyNot.2: The project board does not yet exist when the executive is appointed.

explain.h: Executive versus senior user on benefits
explain.body: The executive owns the business case, secures funding and is accountable for the project's success. The senior user specifies the benefits, shows they are on track and is responsible for their continued realization after the project closes.

test.q: After the first Carrowford Half Marathon closes and is handed to the events team, someone must remain responsible for the continued realization of the expected local spending and participation benefits. Which role is it?
test.why: The senior user is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after the project has closed (6.2.4.2).

whyNot.0: The executive owns the business case and funding, but benefits realization after closure rests with the senior user.
whyNot.2: The project manager's role ends at closure.
whyNot.3: Project assurance advises the board during the project; it is not responsible for realizing benefits after closure.
